title: Your dhikr
tomorrow: Amira stumbles reading Arabic out loud. is the stumbling a problem?

cards: You ask a parent for help and get advice instead. Familiar? Here's an old one, from a report in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, has hands worn sore from turning a hand mill to grind grain. She hears that captives have been brought to her father, and she goes to ask for one to help her with the work.
He isn't home, so she leaves word. That night, she and her husband 'Ali have already lain down when he arrives. He tells them to stay where they are, and sits down between them.

teach.b: Instead he asks: shall I not tell you of something better than what you asked for?
When you lie down, say SubhanAllah thirty-three times, alhamdulillah thirty-three times, and Allahu akbar thirty-four times. That, he says, is better for you than a servant.
So that's what she got: words for the night instead of hands for the day. Tradition calls this set the tasbih of Fatima. Dhikr means remembrance: short phrases said again and again.
Glory to God. Praise to God. God is greater.
The Qur'an says what they do, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Notice what the story doesn't say.
It doesn't say her sore hands were imaginary, or that the work didn't matter. It says that alongside the work, something else could carry her.
And 'Ali, in another report, says he never left those words after that night.

Your dhikr is choosing which remembrances you'll keep, and when: after a prayer, on the bus, at the edge of sleep. One for tonight: the bedtime set people call Fatima's began with a daughter asking her father for help.

how: Muslims say short remembrances after the prayers and through the day, counting on their fingers or on prayer beads (a tasbih or misbaha); the tasbih of Fatima is said at bedtime.

o: the remembrance phrases you choose to keep each day
a long night prayer said once a year in Ramadan
the call to prayer that sounds from a mosque

p: asked for help with the work

s: dhikr is only for long sessions on special nights
Fatima's set is three short phrases at bedtime; dhikr fits anywhere.
in the report, Fatima asked her father for a servant
her hands were sore from the hand mill; he gave her words for the night instead.
the story says Fatima's work didn't matter
it doesn't say that. it says something else could carry her alongside the work.

games.q: it's 1 a.m., you can't sleep, and your phone is right there on the pillow. what fits today's story?
o: scroll until you're tired enough to drop off.
Fatima's three phrases, counted on your fingers in the dark.
get up and plan tomorrow in detail so your mind settles.
games.why: the Prophet gave Fatima those words for when she lay down. 13:28: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest.

practice: Say the three phrases softly, counting on your fingers or on beads: SubhanAllah, glory to God. Alhamdulillah, praise to God. Allahu akbar, God is greater.
Go as far as the time allows; if you'd rather, say the English meanings, and if you lose count, just start the phrase you're on again.

wordCard.voice: Your dhikr: the remembrances you choose to keep each day. Fatima's set came at bedtime.

carryVoice: Your line: my dhikr. Three phrases, light enough to carry anywhere. Three of ten, counted.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3705; Sahih Muslim 2727 (Fatima asks for a servant; the bedtime tasbih)

sources.q: Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!
